title: Focaccia
subtitle: Dimpled flatbread with olive oil, rosemary, and sea salt
excerpt: A thick, pillowy flatbread made with a generous amount of olive oil, dimpled all over before baking, and finished with rosemary and flaky salt. Crisp on the outside, open and airy within.

recipe.sourceNotes: Focaccia is a flatbread from Liguria in north-west Italy, where it has been made since antiquity. The name derives from the Latin focus, meaning hearth, where the original versions were cooked. Ligurian focaccia is thinner and crispier than the thick, dimpled version that became popular globally. The British version uses the latter style, popularised by Californian bakers in the 1990s. The oil is used in three ways: in the dough, poured over the top before baking, and drizzled over immediately after. It should be eaten the day it is made.

content.text: The dough should be very wet and sticky: do not add more flour. The oil in the tin stops it sticking and helps the base crisp. When dimpling, push your fingers all the way through to the bottom of the tin. The focaccia is done when it is deep golden on top and a tap on the base sounds hollow.

Mix the flour, yeast, and fine salt in a large bowl. Add 60 ml of olive oil and 375 ml warm water. Mix to a shaggy, sticky dough. Knead in the bowl for 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Cover and leave to rise in a warm place for 1 hour until doubled.
Pour 20 ml of olive oil into a 30 x 20 cm roasting tin. Tip the dough into the tin. Stretch it to fill the tin as best you can. Cover and leave to prove for 45 minutes.

Heat the oven to 220 C / fan 200 C / gas 7. Drizzle more olive oil over the surface. Dimple the dough vigorously all over with your fingers, pressing all the way to the tin base. Press the rosemary leaves into the dimples. Scatter with flaky salt.
Bake for 20 to 25 minutes until deep golden all over. Drizzle with a little more olive oil while still hot. Cool for 10 minutes before cutting. Eat on the day.
